plan.question: How did a student protest become a national crisis?

chapters.title: The Spark
beats: In Nanterre, a university outside Paris, tensions had been building for months. On 22 March, 150 students occupied an administration building to protest class discrimination. The administration responded by shutting down the campus on 2 May. This closure pushed the conflict to the Sorbonne in central Paris. On 3 May, students gathered at the Sorbonne to protest the Nanterre closure and threatened expulsions. By 6 May, more than 20,000 students and supporters marched toward the Sorbonne. The police charged, leading to clashes, barricades, and hundreds of arrests. De Gaulle watched from the Élysée Palace, seeing not just students, but a challenge to his authority.

The initial confrontation was chaotic. Police used force to disperse the crowd, but the violence only hardened the resolve of the protesters. The Sorbonne became a symbol of resistance. De Gaulle’s government viewed this as a disturbance to be contained, but the scale of the march signaled a deeper fracture in French society.

chapters.title: The Streets
beats: The conflict escalated rapidly on the Rive Gauche. On 10 May, intense street battles erupted after police attacked student barricades. Hundreds were arrested and injured. The situation was deteriorating beyond the government’s control. Pompidou, the Prime Minister, struggled to maintain order while navigating the political fallout. The police, led by the Paris police chief, found themselves overwhelmed by the sheer number of protesters.

On 13 May, the crisis transformed from a student protest into a national strike. A union-led general strike was called, and over a million people marched through Paris. This was no longer just about universities; it was a total social upheaval. The workers joined the students, creating a united front that the government could not easily dismiss. Pompidou realized the magnitude of the threat: the state was paralyzed.

chapters.title: The Flight
beats: This was the moment of maximum vulnerability. The President of France had fled his own palace. The state appeared to have ceased to function. The power vacuum was immediate and terrifying.

chapters.title: The Return
beats: In Baden-Baden, General Jacques Massu learned of the military’s support for de Gaulle. He persuaded the President to return to France. De Gaulle’s return was a turning point. On 30 May, 400,000 to 500,000 protesters marched through Paris, chanting 'Adieu, de Gaulle!'. The police expected only 50,000. The sheer scale of the protest highlighted the depth of popular discontent.
Pompidou, who had stayed in Paris, later recalled the fear of that day. The return of the President restored the legitimacy of the state, but the underlying tensions remained.

chapters.title: The Aftermath
beats: The immediate crisis subsided, but the consequences were profound. On 16 June, the police retook the Sorbonne. On 23 June, the legislative election was held, resulting in a resounding victory for de Gaulle’s party, which won 353 seats. The political threat was neutralized, but the social fabric had changed.

For Mitterrand and the Left, the defeat was a setback, but the movement had secured significant concessions. The Grenelle agreements, negotiated in late May, had secured a 35% minimum wage increase and a 10% salary increase, though unions later rejected them. The events of 1968 weakened de Gaulle’s authority. In 1969, de Gaulle resigned, his power diminished by the earlier crisis. An April referendum in 1969 showed the country was ready for 'Gaullism without de Gaulle'. The movement led to increased state investment in education and social policies, and major concessions in labor rights, including wage increases and better working conditions. The state had survived, but it was forever altered.
